To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) for the first time we determine Be abundances in a large sample of cool stars, (ii) we confirm the existence of a strong Be depletion in these stars, (iii) we do not find a clear evidence that the Be content in stars with planets is lower than that of stars without planets, and (iv) the Be abundance in the stars of the sample is constant for T eff 5500 K.
Be abundances in cool main-sequence stars are strongly depleted, and that this depletion is not related to the presence of planetary companions, at least in the sample of stars studied here.

Be abundances decrease as T eff decreases, with an abrupt fall around 6000 K, and that there are no significant differences between stars with and without known planets in the range of temperatures studied.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is a strong Be depletion at T eff < 6000 K that is independent of the existence of planetary companions, while there is a Li depletion in solar type stars with planets, although the effect is still unclear and needs to be studied further.
there is no evidence for any effect of planets on Be depletion, although this does not mean that the presence of a planetary companion has no influence on the Be abundance of a star.
Be is not depleted more strongly in solar-type stars hosting planets than in stars without detected companions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the depletion of Li and Be is a common feature of all cool stars, but the depletion of Li seems to be more severe than that of Be, especially for solar-type stars with detected planets.
, in the range of effective temperatures covered by our sample, Be abundances do not seem to depend on the presence of planets, although this result needs to be confirmed with more data.
Be depletion is not a simple process and it is strongly affected by stellar evolution and/or the environment of the stars, as it is the case for Li.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Be depletion in cool stars is much more severe than previously thought, and the reason why it is so remains unknown.
Be depletion in solar-type dwarfs is not a continuous process but a step-like process that is triggered around T eff 5500 K.
Be is not a good indicator to distinguish between stars with and without exoplanets.
